triage.name: Fecal impaction
triage.reason: Abdominal pain, distension and inability to pass stool; diagnosed by history, exam and imaging, with bowel obstruction and constipation as look-alikes.

review_issues: exam: term 'Focal neurologic deficit' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: More common in older adults, especially those who are bedbound or in nursing homes
Occurs in children, particularly with toilet training difficulties or withholding behavior
More common in people with limited mobility or neurogenic bowel

risk_factors.text: Neurogenic bowel (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease)
Use of constipating medications (opioids, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers)

social_history: Residence in a nursing home or long-term care facility

chief_complaints.text: I can't poop and my belly hurts
I feel like I need to go but nothing comes out
My stomach is swollen and hard
I have leakage of stool and I can't control it

hpi.onset: Gradual over days to weeks, often on a background of chronic constipation
hpi.duration: Days to weeks of worsening constipation before presentation
hpi.progression: Starts as infrequent hard stools, then no stool passage at all; abdominal pain and distension build up; may develop overflow leakage
hpi.location: Lower abdomen, suprapubic or left lower quadrant
hpi.radiation: Usually none; may be diffuse if severe
hpi.timing: Constant, may worsen after meals or attempts to defecate
relieving: Passing small amounts of liquid stool (overflow)

associated_symptoms.text: No bowel movement for several days

argues_against: Severe constant pain with peritoneal signs
Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin

negatives: Loss of sensation in the perineum

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with overflow diarrhea and soiling rather than clear constipation; they may hide or deny symptoms and have withholding behavior.
missing_classic_features: Clear history of no bowel movement

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, agitation, or urinary retention without reporting constipation; pain may be mild or absent.
Constipation is common in pregnancy; impaction may present with lower abdominal pain and pressure, and must be distinguished from obstetric causes.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable at rest, mild lower abdominal discomfort
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, distended abdomen, prefers to lie still
general.severe: Ill-appearing, distended and tender abdomen, reluctant to move
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, lethargic, with marked abdominal distension

findings.maneuver: Inspect the abdomen from the foot of the bed and measure abdominal girth
findings.finding: Visible abdominal distension, tympanitic to percussion

findings.maneuver: Palpate the lower abdomen and left lower quadrant deeply
findings.finding: Palpable firm, nontender or mildly tender mass in the lower abdomen or left lower quadrant

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, starting away from the area of maximal discomfort
findings.finding: Mild to moderate tenderness, most often suprapubic or left lower quadrant

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position
findings.finding: Hard, firm stool mass palpable in the rectal vault, often filling the rectal ampulla

findings.maneuver: Assess anal sphincter tone during the digital rectal exam
findings.finding: Normal or reduced anal sphincter tone; may be lax in neurogenic bowel

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to cough, then gently percuss and release pressure over the abdomen
findings.finding: No rebound tenderness or involuntary guarding

findings.maneuver: Inspect the examining glove and stool for blood after the digital rectal exam
findings.finding: No gross blood on the glove or stool

findings.maneuver: Inspect the sclerae and skin in natural light
Test perineal sensation and lower extremity strength and reflexes
findings.finding: No saddle anesthesia, lower extremity weakness, or reduced reflexes

labs.caveat: A normal white count is expected in uncomplicated impaction; leukocytosis suggests a complication such as ischemia, perforation, or an alternative diagnosis.
Rises with dehydration from poor intake or vomiting.
Prerenal elevation from dehydration; also relevant before giving osmotic laxatives or enemas.
Hypokalemia from laxative overuse or vomiting.
Low bicarbonate suggests a metabolic acidosis and raises concern for bowel ischemia.
An elevated lactate with severe pain or peritoneal signs suggests bowel ischemia or perforation rather than simple impaction.
Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of chronic constipation and should be checked when no obvious cause is found.
Hypercalcemia causes constipation and altered mental status, especially in older adults.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line when obstruction or perforation is a concern; widely available and quick

findings.text: Large amount of fecal material in the rectum and distal colon
Dilated loops of colon proximal to the fecal burden

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is unclear, obstruction or ischemia is suspected, or the patient does not improve with treatment

findings.text: Impacted fecal mass distending the rectum or distal colon
Proximal colonic dilation with feces and gas
Colonic wall thickening or stranding suggesting ischemia or colitis
Free air or abscess suggesting perforation

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When ischemia, perforation, or abscess is suspected and renal function permits

findings.text: Impacted fecal mass with surrounding inflammatory change
Bowel wall hypoenhancement or pneumatosis suggesting ischemia
Abscess or extraluminal air suggesting perforation

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected colonic obstruction or when therapeutic enema is planned

findings.text: Fecal mass outlined by contrast in the rectum or sigmoid
Narrowed or obstructing lesion if a stricture or tumor is present

initial.why: Baseline white count; leukocytosis suggests a complication or another diagnosis
Assesses dehydration, electrolytes, and renal function before laxatives or enemas
Confirms fecal burden and screens for obstruction or perforation

confirmatory.test: CT abdomen and pelvis without IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Defines the fecal mass and excludes obstruction, ischemia, or perforation when the picture is atypical or the patient is not improving

supporting.only_if: no clear cause of constipation or symptoms are chronic
older adult with confusion or unexplained constipation
severe pain, peritoneal signs, or toxic appearance

supporting.why: Can confirm and sometimes relieve a distal obstruction
supporting.only_if: obstruction is suspected or therapeutic enema is planned

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless pain is epigastric or pancreatitis is suspected
No role in constipation or abdominal distension
Limited by gas and does not characterize a fecal mass well
Not for acute impaction; reserved for bleeding, weight loss, or suspected tumor after the impaction is cleared

decision_points: Digital rectal exam is the key bedside step; a hard stool mass in the rectal vault confirms the diagnosis
Fever, peritoneal signs, or an elevated lactate should prompt imaging for ischemia or perforation rather than simple disimpaction
Check renal function and electrolytes before giving osmotic laxatives or enemas in frail or dehydrated patients
In children, consider Hirschsprung disease or withholding behavior if impaction recurs

differential.name: Small bowel obstruction
differential.why_considered: Abdominal pain, distension, vomiting and inability to pass stool or gas
differential.trigger: Bilious vomiting, high-pitched or absent bowel sounds, and dilated small bowel loops on imaging

history: Colicky periumbilical pain that comes in waves
Vomiting that is bilious or feculent and precedes the distension
Prior abdominal surgery with adhesions
exam: Tympanitic distension with tenderness but no palpable stool mass
Empty rectal vault on digital exam
labs: Elevated lactate and metabolic acidosis if strangulated
Elevated BUN and creatinine from dehydration
imaging: Dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels on abdominal x-ray
Transition point with collapsed distal bowel on CT

differential.name: Colorectal cancer
differential.why_considered: Progressive constipation, abdominal pain and distension in an older adult, sometimes with a distal obstructing lesion
differential.trigger: Weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, rectal bleeding, or a new change in bowel habit in an older adult

history: Weeks to months of progressive constipation
Unintentional weight loss
Blood in stool or a change in stool caliber
exam: Palpable firm mass that is not stool and does not change after disimpaction
labs: Iron deficiency anemia with low ferritin
Occult blood positive on stool testing
imaging: Apple-core or shouldered stricture on contrast enema
Colonic wall thickening or mass with lymphadenopathy on CT

differential.name: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction
differential.why_considered: Marked abdominal distension with absent bowel movements in a hospitalized or bedbound patient
differential.trigger: Massive colonic dilation without a mechanical obstruction on CT, especially after surgery or in a critically ill patient

history: Recent surgery, trauma, or critical illness
Use of opioids or anticholinergics
Distension out of proportion to pain
exam: Tympanitic, distended abdomen with mild tenderness
Rectal vault may be empty or contain only small amounts of soft stool
labs: Electrolyte abnormalities such as hypokalemia or hypocalcemia
Normal white count unless ischemia develops
imaging: Dilated colon with a normal transition at the splenic flexure and no obstructing lesion on CT
Absent fecal mass in the rectum

differential.name: Diverticulitis
differential.why_considered: Left lower quadrant pain, fever and altered bowel habits in an older adult

history: Acute onset of constant left lower quadrant pain
Fever and chills
Diarrhea or constipation with nausea
exam: Focal left lower quadrant tenderness with guarding
No hard stool mass in the rectal vault
imaging: Colonic diverticula with pericolic fat stranding and wall thickening on CT

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome with constipation
differential.why_considered: Chronic constipation, abdominal pain and bloating in an otherwise well patient

history: Long-standing alternating constipation and diarrhea
Pain relieved by defecation
No weight loss, bleeding, or nocturnal symptoms
exam: Mild diffuse tenderness without a palpable mass
Normal digital rectal exam without a stool mass
imaging: Normal abdominal x-ray or CT without a fecal burden

differential.name: Hirschsprung disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic constipation and abdominal distension in an infant or young child, sometimes with overflow soiling

history: Delay in passing meconium beyond 48 hours of life
Chronic constipation since infancy
Failure to thrive
exam: Distended abdomen with a tight anal sphincter
Empty rectal vault on digital exam with a gush of stool after withdrawal
labs: Normal electrolytes unless enterocolitis is present
imaging: Transition zone on contrast enema with a narrowed aganglionic segment
Rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells

differential.name: Medication-induced constipation
differential.why_considered: Constipation and abdominal discomfort temporally related to constipating drugs

history: Recent initiation or dose increase of opioids, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, or iron
Symptoms improve with medication adjustment
exam: Mild abdominal tenderness without a fixed mass
Rectal vault may be empty or contain soft stool
imaging: Fecal burden on x-ray without obstruction

severity.mild: Recent impaction with mild lower abdominal discomfort, no distension, and a palpable rectal stool mass; able to eat and drink
severity.moderate: Established impaction with abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and incomplete evacuation; may have overflow soiling
severity.severe: Marked distension and pain with vomiting, dehydration, or urinary retention; requires urgent disimpaction and monitoring
severity.critical: Impaction complicated by bowel ischemia, perforation, or sepsis with peritoneal signs, hypotension, or altered mental status

red_flags.finding: Fever with focal or diffuse abdominal tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests ischemia, perforation, or an alternative diagnosis such as diverticulitis

red_flags.finding: Peritoneal signs (rebound tenderness, involuntary guarding, rigid abdomen)
red_flags.meaning: Concern for perforation or peritonitis; needs urgent surgical evaluation
Suggests bowel obstruction rather than simple impaction

red_flags.finding: Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status)
red_flags.meaning: Possible sepsis or hypovolemia from vomiting and poor intake
Raises concern for ischemia, tumor, or severe mucosal injury
Large pelvic stool mass compressing the bladder; needs urgent decompression

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, agitation, or urinary retention rather than reporting constipation; pain may be mild or absent, and complications are more likely.
Often presents with overflow diarrhea and soiling rather than clear constipation; withholding behavior and Hirschsprung disease should be considered.
Constipation is common in pregnancy; impaction may cause lower abdominal pain and pressure that must be distinguished from obstetric causes.
Higher risk of severe infection or perforation; fever and tenderness should be evaluated urgently.
Avoid magnesium- or phosphate-containing enemas; adjust osmotic laxative doses and monitor electrolytes closely.

key_questions.question: When was your last bowel movement, and how often do you normally go?
key_questions.looking_for: Several days or longer without a bowel movement against a background of chronic constipation

key_questions.question: Have you been passing any gas?
key_questions.looking_for: Passing gas suggests impaction; absent gas with distension raises concern for obstruction

key_questions.question: Do you feel like you need to go but nothing comes out?
key_questions.looking_for: Tenesmus and a sensation of incomplete evacuation

key_questions.question: Have you had any leakage of stool or liquid that you cannot control?
key_questions.looking_for: Overflow soiling or fecal incontinence, which is easily mistaken for diarrhea

key_questions.question: Any nausea, vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting, especially bilious, suggests obstruction rather than simple impaction

key_questions.question: Any blood in your stool or black tarry stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Bleeding raises concern for ischemia, tumor, or stercoral ulceration

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, or severe constant pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or severe pain suggests ischemia, perforation, or an alternative diagnosis

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, especially pain medicines, anticholinergics, or iron?
key_questions.looking_for: Opioids, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, aluminum or calcium antacids, and iron

key_questions.question: Do you have any conditions that affect your bowels or nerves, such as Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, or dementia?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurogenic bowel or cognitive impairment predisposing to impaction

key_questions.question: How much fluid and fiber do you get, and how active are you?
key_questions.looking_for: Low fluid or fiber intake and immobility or bedbound status

key_questions.question: Have you had abdominal surgery or been told you have diverticular disease or a bowel stricture?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior surgery, adhesions, or strictures that predispose to obstruction

key_questions.question: Any trouble urinating or a feeling of not emptying your bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary retention from a large pelvic stool mass compressing the bladder

reasoning_points: Chronic constipation with several days or more without a bowel movement
Abdominal pain and distension with a sensation of incomplete evacuation
Overflow leakage of liquid stool or fecal incontinence, which can be mistaken for diarrhea
A hard, firm stool mass palpable in the rectal vault on digital rectal examination
A palpable firm lower abdominal or left lower quadrant mass
Absence of peritoneal signs, fever, and gross blood in an uncomplicated case
Abdominal imaging showing a large fecal burden in the rectum or distal colon
Exclusion of obstruction, ischemia, perforation, and colorectal cancer

easy: Older bedbound or nursing home patient with chronic constipation and no bowel movement for days
Abdominal distension with a palpable firm lower abdominal mass
Hard stool mass felt in the rectal vault on digital rectal exam
Abdominal x-ray showing a large fecal burden
medium: Older adult presenting with confusion, agitation, or urinary retention rather than reporting constipation
Overflow soiling or leakage of liquid stool mistaken for diarrhea
Patient on opioids or anticholinergics with new abdominal pain and distension
Mild leukocytosis or dehydration requiring evaluation before disimpaction
hard: Child with overflow diarrhea and soiling rather than clear constipation, raising concern for Hirschsprung disease
Pregnant patient with lower abdominal pain and pressure that must be distinguished from obstetric causes
Impaction complicated by obstruction, ischemia, or perforation with fever, peritoneal signs, or elevated lactate
Older adult with progressive constipation and weight loss where colorectal cancer must be excluded
